Today through Tuesday: The potent upper level low that brought 
showers and thunderstorms and gusty winds to the Inland Northwest on 
Saturday will be making its exit today. Wrap around moisture will 
continue to bring light rain to portions of northeast Washington 
into the Northern Panhandle will bring light rain through the 
morning. It will exit by the afternoon with a few weakly forced 
convective showers lingering over far north Idaho for the afternoon. 
Today will continue to be a bit breezy, but not nearly as gusty as 
Saturday. Expect sustained winds of up to around 12 mph with gusts 
up to around 20 mph for exposed areas of the Columbia Basin. 
Temperatures remain below normal today with highs in the 70s.

Shortwave ridging of higher pressure for Monday into Tuesday will 
result in a rebound in our temperatures. Highs will warm 5-12 degrees 
from Sunday into Monday back into the 80s. Winds will be light under 
the ridge and conditions will dry out considerably. This will be 
especially so across the southeast portion of the forecast area 
where a pocket of relatively drier air migrates in over the region. 
Absent of much wind, these drier conditions don't look to pose much 
of a fire weather threat. It may provide an opportunity for current 
active fires to perk back up and produce smoke again. The ridge axis 
begins to shift east of the region on Tuesday with longwave trough 
of lower pressure digging down off of the west coast. The flow 
pattern will back result in a warmer, more moist southerly flow 
orientation. Temperatures will see additional rises into Tuesday 
with the southerly flow advecting in warmer temperatures aloft. 
Increased moisture will also bring across high level clouds, but not 
enough to counteract the effects of the warm air advection on our 
temperatures.

Tuesday night through Thursday night: The pattern changes for mid 
week with more fall like weather expected. Before this transition 
occurs though, we will be watching the potential for lightning. A 
negatively tilted shortwave trough will swing up across the region 
for Tuesday night into Wednesday. There are some timing differences 
among the model ensembles that need to be ironed out for better 
confidence on timing; however, the three ingredients for storms look 
to be coming together after a brief warm up generates low level heat 
and increasing moisture sets up an increasingly unstable situation 
paired with a dynamic negatively tilted shortwave. We could see 
storms as early as Tuesday night, or they may hold off more into 
Wednesday morning into Wednesday afternoon. Thunderstorms will be 
capable of lightning strikes that start new fires as well as gusty 
outflow winds. The consensus reflects timing of the shortwave to be 
more early day on Wednesday that would limit the potential for 
stronger storms Wednesday afternoon. Southerly winds pick up on 
Wednesday as well, and may be enhanced by convection. Stronger winds 
with gusts up to 30-35 mph looks to be across the western Columbia 
Basin and up the Okanogan Valley.

Models begin to diverge a bit with a second shortwave Wednesday 
night into Thursday. This disturbance is expected to be a better 
rain producer with additional time for the atmosphere to moisten up. 
The question is where the deformation band sets up and will it track 
across the Inland Northwest. Some of the ensembles members are less 
bullish in swing it all the across into the Idaho Panhandle. The 
potential for wetting rains looks favorable with this frontal system 
though. The NBM goes as far as a 50-70% chance for at least a 
quarter of an inch of precipitation across the mountains. It would 
be a welcome sight for the current fire situation.

Friday through Sunday: Model ensembles diverge further heading into 
the next weekend. There is general agreement that the trough will be 
slow moving to push across the region. Some ensembles wants to pinch 
off a closed low circulation and have it retrograde out into the 
eastern Pacific. This scenario would act to pump the Four Corners 
High up a bit more with temperatures warmer than in the forecast. 
The NBM calls for decreasing chances of precipitation and 
temperatures generally warming closer to normal for early September. 
/SVH
